slides.title: Indigenous Skills and Employment Training (ISET) Orientation Guidance Modules 2025-2026

content.text: Indigenous Skills and Employment Training (ISET) Orientation Guidance Modules 2025-2026

items: This in-tool guidance is written for ISET Coordinators/Case Managers doing day-to-day intake, assessment, approvals, payments, and case management.

File lifecycle reference (use as a checklist — not every client file includes every step, and some steps repeat when information is missing): Digital application intake received → assign to the appropriate Regional Manager (automatic or manual) → Regional Manager may reassign to an ISET Coordinator → Program Administrator initiates EI eligibility verification and records the outcome (only after obtaining the required client consent; if consent is missing, request it) → assigned staff sign a Conflict of Interest declaration before substantive review → Program Administrator evaluates any declared conflict and either clears it or reassigns the application → request missing documents (repeat until complete or close) → confirm overall eligibility → assess employability needs → develop/confirm action plan + intervention → submit recommendation → NWAC decision → funding agreement → deliver supports/payments (track attendance and receipts where applicable) → follow-up and file closure → reporting (including ILMP submissions through the ESDC portal when an action plan/intervention is activated and when it is closed, as applicable).

What “not every file includes every step” means in practice: Some files end early (e.g., ineligible or incomplete). Some steps repeat (e.g., requesting missing documents, revising an action plan, or updating a recommendation). Some steps are conditional (e.g., EI verification only when applicable and only with the required consent; attendance tracking only when a support requires it). If a conflict of interest is declared, the file is reassigned before work continues.
Tip: When you’re unsure, document your reasoning in the client file and escalate early (before committing funding).
Module 1 sets the foundation: who delivers ISET under NWAC, what the program is for, and the eligibility/identity rules that must be satisfied before a file can move forward.

In April 2019, NWAC signed a ten-year Contribution Agreement with Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) to deliver the Indigenous Skills and Employment Training (ISET) program. This program and the current funding are scheduled to end on March 31, 2029.
The Contribution Agreement that NWAC holds with ESDC is valued at approximately $33,000,000 over the term of the Agreement.
There are two annual funding streams within the Contribution Agreement:
↳ Employment Insurance (EI) – for those clients eligible to be funded under the Employment Insurance Program.
↳ Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF) – for those clients or expenses that are not eligible to be funded under EI.
↳ ESDC sets the amounts eligible under the EI Stream.
↳ Funds from the CRF stream can be reallocated to the EI stream but the reverse is not permissible.
In practice: EI vs CRF affects both who can be funded and what costs can be paid. Confirm the stream early so you don’t have to unwind approvals later.
Plain-language refresher: EI in this context is typically tied to EI Part II eligibility (training measures), which is different from being on an active EI Part I benefit claim.
Tip: Document the EI/CRF determination (and how it was obtained) in case notes in the client file so the file is self-explanatory for reviews and audits.
NWAC - Native Women’s Association of Canada
Established in 1974 (50th year in 2024)

We were founded on the collective goal to enhance, promote, and foster the social, economic, cultural, and political well-being of Indigenous women and girls within their respective communities and Canadian societies. NWAC also defends the rights, delivers programming to, and amplifies the perspectives of Indigenous women in their diversities.
NWAC is inclusive of First Nations—on- and off-reserve, status, non-status, and disenfranchised—Inuit, and Métis.
PTMA - Provincial Territorial Membership Association
Member organization that support the work of NWAC.
13 grassroots organizations in every province and territory in Canada.
Currently 10 women’s organizations after SK, NL and PE were removed in October 2024.
NWAC has the discretion to sign sub-agreements with a PTMA to help deliver the ISET program nationally in their region.
In practice: Know who your escalation path is (PTMA lead / NWAC National Office) for eligibility edge cases, exceptions, and approvals.
Tip: Use consistent language when describing NWAC, PTMAs, and service delivery roles so clients understand who is making decisions and why.
ISET Holders are Indigenous organizations that have the designated authority through Contribution Agreements with ESDC to act on behalf of Canada in the delivery of the ISET program.
There are approximately 115 regional ISET holders across Canada. The Native Women’s Association of Canada (NWAC) is one of two national ISET Holders.

The Native Women’s Association of Canada (NWAC) provides employment and training support services across Canada to Indigenous women and girls in all their diversities. The National Office provides overall coordination, administration and auditing of its program in all provinces and territories to ensure compliance with all aspects of the program.
Where applicable, and through sub-agreements, NWAC works in collaboration with our Provincial-Territorial Member Associations (PTMAs), to deliver the program regionally/territorially.
Day-to-day: Your case file should reflect that NWAC is the agreement holder and you are delivering services under NWAC guidelines and the contribution agreement.
Tip: When referring clients elsewhere (other holders or services), note the reason and outcome in the client file (program system) to preserve continuity of service.

The Mandate of the ISETs program is to increase Indigenous participation in the Canadian labour market. The program supports First Nations, Metis and Inuit persons with access to sustainable and meaningful employment by closing the employment and earnings gaps between Indigenous and non-Indigenous people by placing greater emphasis on training and education.

The ISET program provides access to training and employment supports to Canadian Indigenous women in their diversities, including status and non-status First Nations, Metis and Inuit peoples whether residing on or off-reserve, in urban centres and in rural, remote communities.

The ISET program is intended to provide financial supports such as tuition, living allowance, childcare, job starts and other resources to help eligible Indigenous women in all their diversities to reach their employment and skills training goals.
Client-facing framing: ISET exists to help clients reach sustainable employment through training and supports—connect funding decisions back to the employment goal.
Coordinator tip: When recommending costs, tie each cost to a barrier or requirement of the intervention (e.g., tuition required for credential; childcare required to attend).
Canadian citizen
Indigenous women in all their diversities
↳ status and non-status First Nations, Metis and Inuit peoples whether residing on or off-reserve, in urban centres and in rural, remote communities
Be unemployed, under-employed, or can demonstrate an immediate risk of becoming unemployed.
Active NWAC or PTMA staff (including Board members) are NOT eligible to receive funding under the ISET program or by its partner organizations.
Decision gate: If a client does not meet eligibility requirements, pause processing and document the determination (and communication) clearly.
Tip: ‘At risk of unemployment’ should be documented with a brief rationale (e.g., seasonal work ending, reduced hours, layoff notice).
Every applicant that applies for ISET funding MUST provide a copy of their Status, Treaty or Nation card and must also sign the ‘Self-Declaration’ form.
Signing only the ‘Self-Declaration’ is not sufficient.

Where no documentation has be provided, the onus will be on that individual to obtain the necessary documentation to support their claim of Indigenous identity/community connection, including but not limited to two (2) letters of reference from Indigenous leadership from their Band or Nation.
An individual may also provide historical information regarding lack of status, disenfranchisement and/or Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) form that verifies Indigenous identity, status or heritage.
Privacy tip: Treat identity documentation as highly sensitive—upload securely to the program system and avoid emailing ID unless you’re following your approved secure process.
When no card is available: document what was provided (e.g., reference letters, ISC verification) and why it is sufficient under NWAC guidance.
Indigenous Self-Declaration
Practical reminder: The self-declaration supports identity confirmation but does not replace required ID documentation—keep both in the file.
Tip: Ensure the self-declaration form is fully signed/dated and stored in the client file (program system) with the identity documents.
Module 2 is about choosing and justifying interventions and funding streams—your recommendation should always connect the intervention to an employability outcome.
What is an Intervention?
↳ An Individualized Action Plan activity
↳ Is developed between the Client and the Case Manager
↳ Has a specific timeframe
↳ Intended to help a client improve their skills and employability
↳ Enables them to fully participate in the Canadian economy.
In practice: An intervention should have (1) a goal, (2) start/end dates, (3) required supports, and (4) an expected employment outcome.
Tip: Capture the intervention plan in the file using simple language: “Client will complete X by Y date to qualify for Z job.”
↳ ↳ As the Case Manager, it is your role to conduct appropriate research or assessment of the client’s career/educational or training choice which includes but is not limited to:
↳ Developing informed and realistic career plans and guiding the client towards appropriate resources;
↳ Assisting the client to understand the physical and/or mental challenges associated with different occupations;
↳ Considering career paths that are emerging or are in high demand and discussing the wage scale and ability to progress within the occupation (technology, AI, red seal trades, etc.);
↳ Ensuring the client obtains the necessary skills required (competencies) and credentials to help increase their participation in the Canadian labour force;
↳ Verifying that the program leads to viable employment opportunities in a related field;
↳ Has the potential to help close the earnings gap between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples.
Tip: Treat ‘research’ as evidence for your recommendation—labour market demand, wage expectations, credential requirements, and the realism of the client’s plan.
Good documentation standard: include 2–3 concrete research points (e.g., postings, regulatory body requirements, wage range) rather than general statements.

“As Assessment by the Case Manager of the skills identified by the client to make an informed career choice. In making the assessment, you are required to determine if the client has a realistic goal and the ability to research alternative occupational choices.”
↳ Career Research and Exploration
↳ Diagnostic Assessment
Coordinator tip: If a client can’t clearly explain their goal or pathway, consider career exploration activities before committing to long training.
Evidence examples: notes from career exploration, diagnostic results, and a summary of alternative options discussed.
“Provides clients with the necessary skills and qualifications that are needed to enter and perform in a chosen occupation by enrolling them in the appropriate training or education program.”
Skills Development
↳ Essential Skills;
↳ Academic Upgrading.
Occupational Skills Training:
↳ Degree; Diploma;
↳ Certificate; Apprenticeship;
↳ Industry Recognized.
Work Experience
↳ Student Employment;
↳ Wage Subsidy;
↳ Job Creation Partnerships.
Self-Employment (SEB)
Practical use: map the intervention to the specific skill/credential the occupation requires (essential skills → upgrading → occupational training).
Tip: If you recommend work experience (TWS/JCP), document what skills the placement will build and how it leads to employment.
Client MUST provide a current resume with their ISET application.
As the case manager, you can use the resume both as a verification tool and a conversation starter for career exploration and planning.
Foundation for Assessment
↳ Show’s applicant’s prior education, training and work experience
Supports Career Planning
↳ Helps align training requests with meaningful employment goals
↳ Identifies transferable skills and strengths
Guides Case Management
↳ Case Manager’s can suggest diagnostic testing if gaps are identified
↳ Ensures career goals are realistic and achievable
Exploring Alternatives
↳ Resume review helps consider other occupational choices suited to abilities
File quality tip: Use the resume to cross-check application dates, employment history, and gaps—then ensure case notes in the client file match what the resume shows.
Client support tip: For new staff, build a consistent resume review script (goal, gaps, transferable skills, next steps).
Multiple interventions may be available to clients:
Provided that each intervention supports the needs assessment and employment goals of the client;
When labour market conditions are such that a client cannot find suitable employment in the training occupation;
Provided that the additional training will improve the person’s employment potential.
In practice: Multiple interventions must each have their own rationale, timeframe, and expected employment impact—avoid “stacking” supports without clear purpose.
Tip: Document why the first intervention was insufficient or how labour market conditions changed.
The Individual Training Purchase
Provides clients with the necessary skills and qualifications that are needed to enter and perform within a chosen occupation by enrolling them in the appropriate training or educational program
Provides financial assistance to eligible clients to help pay for the cost of education, skills training courses, related program expenses and living expenses.
Searchable database of over 10,000 academic programs offered leading to an undergraduate or graduate degree from a recognized degree-granting institution: http://oraweb.aucc.ca/dcu_e.html.
ITP tip: Before recommending, confirm the institution/program is recognized/accredited and the credential leads to a real hiring pathway.
Resource note: If a specific program directory link is outdated, use current official institution directories or provincial/territorial registries to confirm accreditation.
Documentation tip: Keep the Letter of Acceptance, Statement of Fees, and proof of required materials together in the client file (program system) under a clear naming convention.
Targeted Wage Subsidy

A financial assistance program which encourages employers to hire individuals for a specific length of time, with the objective of providing the client with on-the-job training and sufficient skills to obtain employment.

Employers are considered as program partners and must focus on providing appropriate orientation and training that support employment, training and goals of the client. Non-profit organizations are eligible for maximum subsidy. Private sector employers are eligible for 50% of wages, MERCs and vacation pay.
Employer must provide a detailed employment plan, including a defined orientation period and job description.

Student Employment - intended to help provide employment to students with the opportunity to develop and enhance employability and occupational skills with practical on-the-job experience. Student must be enrolled in full-time studies.
TWS tip: Employers are partners—your file should show that the employer will provide training/supervision and that there is a pathway to continued employment.
Calculation tip: Record your wage subsidy math (hourly rate × hours × weeks + MERCs/vacation) so another staff member can replicate it.
Required Documents
Employer:
1) Letter stating what employment duties would be;
2) Letter of offer after the Targeted Wage Subsidy is over;
Case Managers cannot move forward with a Targeted Wage Subsidy application without these documents from the employer.
The base amount per hour depends on the Province/Territory but cannot be less than the minimum wage in that specific region.
Subsidy can support up to 8 hours per day.
MERCS – The employer determines the MERCS (this amount is dependent on the amount of money you are recommending to pay per hour).
Practical rule: Do not proceed with a TWS recommendation until the employer documents are in-hand (duties + post-subsidy offer).
Tip: Confirm the wage meets regional minimum wage and that hours do not exceed 8/day as per the program guidance.
The Job Creation Partnership (JCP)
Provides financial assistance to enable unemployed persons to gain work experience by creating temporary jobs.
Project activities should benefit both the participant client and the community
Partnerships with public sector and non-profit employers are allowed – NO private companies
Aim is to improve the client’s long-term employment prospects
JCP tip: Confirm the project benefits the community and builds employability skills—not just temporary work.
Compliance habit: Ensure the employer is public sector or non-profit (no private companies) and document that verification in the file.
The Self-Employment Benefits
Program provides direct financial assistance, business training or professional support to enable a client to start their own business or continue in a career of self-employment
Assistance may include support for:
↳ Training in business start-up and development from an accredited business school;
↳ Business Plan development;
↳ Professional advice for marketing, accounting and financial management, and office location (e.g., incubators)

* Incubators are designed to accelerate the development of a small start-up by partnering within a bigger business, thereby reducing start-up costs, access to experts and lateral contributions such as office supplies, furniture, etc.
SEB tip: Use SEB when the client has a realistic self-employment pathway and is ready for structured business planning and support.
Documentation tip: Your file should include a business plan outline and what professional supports (training, marketing/accounting advice) will be provided.
Funding is available for regionally-based community projects which support employment training and work experience
Eligible projects must provide a combination of certification, life skills, pre-employment skills or practical work experience.

Non-Profit organizations and private corporations must demonstrate capacity to provide the required management, supervision, coordination, financial report and necessary liability insurance for the project.
Funding up to a maximum of 52 weeks
Group training tip: These projects work best with a strong sponsor—document management capacity, supervision plan, and liability/insurance up front.
Planning tip: Track outcomes (certifications earned, job placements) so reporting is easier later.

chunks.title: Module 3 — Your role: delivery, case management, planning, outreach

items: Module 3 covers your role beyond approvals: case management cadence, relationship-based delivery, outreach, and partnerships.

Coordinate service delivery activities and manage the day-to-day operations of the ISET program in your assigned region(s) and support PTMA in accordance with the ESDC Contribution Agreement, program eligibility criteria and NWAC guidelines:
Develop an Annual Regional Workplan
Process Applications for Funding
Provide Direct Case Management to Clients
Build Partnerships with Employers and Educational and Training Institutions
Provide Outreach to Communities – Cultural Protocols
Promote Program Awareness
Ensure Compliance with Data Management Protocols
Support PTMAs /ISET Coordinator within your region on the above activities.
Day-to-day: This role is equal parts file processing and relationship-based service delivery—build routines that keep both moving (e.g., weekly file review + outreach blocks).
Tip: Keep a simple weekly dashboard: pending files, missing docs, approvals awaiting NWAC, payments due, and clients needing check-ins.
What are your Key Priorities/Goals and the specific activities and timelines to achieve your goals?
What are your strategies to meet targets and how will you track your progress?
What are your strategies for engaging employers and building partnerships?
What Communities, regional events, job fairs will you attend to raise awareness of the ISET program?
What educational or training partners will you engage to support your ISET clients?
Budgeting, Forecasting and Financial Reporting
Identify any anticipated challenges/barriers and the mitigation strategies you will employ.
Workplan tip: Write goals that are measurable (e.g., # of intakes processed, # interventions started, # employer partners engaged).
Operational tip: Review and update your workplan quarterly so it stays usable—not just a once-a-year document.
Workplan Template
Use this template as your planning anchor. Keep a working copy and store the approved version where your team can access it.
Program system and client file
↳ Create Client File (Add client info. / New Intake to make “active”)
↳ Upload documents and record interactions
Intake & Needs Assessment
↳ Conduct thorough review of client application
↳ Collect documentation
Individualized Intervention
↳ Understand client’s long-term training and employment goals
↳ Work with client to set expectation and achievable goals
Practical approach: start the client file first, then do needs assessment and document collection—this prevents lost information and supports continuity.
Tip: Set expectations early: what documents are required, what the decision timeline is, and what ‘pending’ means.
As the ISET Case Manager your responsibility to the Client DOES NOT end when a determination has been made to fund a Client application.
During the Client’s entire Intervention, you are the client’s Case Manager.
Client service reminder: Funding is not the end—case management continues through the full intervention (and includes follow-up after completion).
Tip: Build a cadence: monthly check-ins minimum, plus extra touchpoints at start, mid-point, and end.
↳ Regular check-ins (minimum monthly); some clients may require more or less support, throughout their intervention;
↳ support active listening – know and understand your client/needs
↳ Be trauma informed:
↳ ↳ Recognize how colonialization, residential schools, systemic racism and intergenerational trauma continue to affect individuals, families and communities today.
↳ ↳ ensure your approach to services, supports or interactions are rooted in safety, respect and cultural awareness.
Trauma-informed practice: focus on safety, choice, collaboration, trust, and empowerment—especially when discussing barriers.
Practical tip: Use a short monthly check-in structure: attendance/progress → barriers → supports/referrals → next steps → document in the client file (program system).
↳ Record client updates and interactions in the client file (program system)
↳ Monitor attendance at school, training or work placements (TWS/JCP), using absences as an opportunity to check-in and provide support
↳ Track key dates (start, milestones, and end of intervention) to anticipate support needs
↳ Celebrate client achievements and progress along the way
↳ Document outcomes and consider opportunities for further support, including multiple interventions, if appropriate
Tip: Treat absences as a support signal, not a compliance trigger—check in early to prevent disengagement.
Record-keeping tip: Log milestones and key dates so you can anticipate payment needs, reporting, and follow-up timelines.
↳ Connect clients to appropriate community resources and services (e.g., mental health, family supports, housing, domestic violence, addictions, etc.
↳ Recognize professional boundaries – client case managers are not expected to provide direct counselling but to make referrals and ensure clients are supported
↳ Adapt the intervention if a client’s personal circumstances require a change in direction
↳ Encourage open communication so clients feel comfortable sharing challenges or barriers that may affect their progress
↳ Collaborate with partners (training institutions, employers, service providers) to help address barriers and maintain client engagement
Boundary tip: You are not expected to provide counselling—your job is to connect clients to appropriate supports and document the referral/outcome.
Safety note: If a client discloses safety risks (violence, housing insecurity), prioritize immediate referral pathways and document only what is necessary.

slides.title: Client Case Management Follow-up and File Closure

items: ↳ Conduct follow-ups with the client during the 12-weeks following the end of their intervention to confirm their status (employed, unemployed but looking for work, return to school, etc.)
↳ Track long-term outcomes to assess the effectiveness of the intervention and identify future support needs
↳ Invite clients (if they are comfortable) to share a success story through video, letter or social media to highlight their ISET journey
↳ Complete proper closure of the intervention in the client file (program system) to ensure files are not left ‘active’, and with a clear determination recorded at the end of every intervention
Outcome tip: Define closure outcomes consistently (employed, returned to school, unemployed seeking work, etc.) and record them in the client file (program system).
Client-centered tip: Invite success stories only with informed consent; never pressure clients to share.
Research & Targeting
↳ Identify employers/training providers in your region(s) that align with client goals, training and employment pathways
Initial Outreach
↳ Introduce ISET, share benefits and success stories
Relationship Building
↳ Meet, listen, and find common ground
Collaboration Opportunities
↳ Co-host career fairs, training, pipelines / develop cohorts
Maintain Engagement
↳ Provide updates, acknowledge contributions, cultural training
Partnership tip: Start with 3–5 priority employers/providers aligned to your most common client pathways, then deepen relationships over time.
Documentation tip: Keep partnership notes (contacts, meetings, commitments) in a consistent place so your team can maintain continuity.

slides.title: Outreach to Indigenous Communities: Awareness & Cultural Protocols

items: Community Research
↳ Learn about the community's history, leadership, priorities
Respect Protocols
↳ Ask about and follow cultural customs for introductions, gifting, and meetings
Engage Elders & Knowledge Keepers
↳ Seek guidance and permission to present
Culturally Relevant Messaging
↳ Highlight how ISET aligns with community values
Presence & Relationship
↳ Attend community events if invited (if possible), not just program promotion
Follow-Up & Trust
↳ Set expectations, provide updates, honor commitments, maintain respectful relationships
Protocol tip: Ask communities how they prefer to be engaged—who to contact, how to introduce yourself, and what protocols to follow.
Trust-building tip: Follow up after events with updates and kept promises—this is often more important than the initial presentation.
Pre-Event Research
↳ Understand audience, venue, and other exhibitors
Materials
↳ Bring brochures, success stories (with permission), application forms, cultural items as appropriate
Visual Appeal
↳ Use banners, posters, and culturally relevant displays
Key Messaging
↳ Focus on benefits: skills training, employment pathways, supports, if eligible
Engagement
↳ Offer interactive elements, answer questions, collect contact info
Follow-Up
↳ Send information to leads, maintain engagement after the event
Practical tip: Always capture leads (name, contact, interest) and create a lightweight follow-up routine within 48–72 hours after events.
Messaging tip: Focus on outcomes (“training that leads to work”) and supports (“help removing barriers”), then screen for eligibility.

chunks.title: Module 4 — Intake and processing: EI verification and program records

items: Module 4 is the operational core: intake sources, EI verification, the program system setup, and processing timelines.
↳ Client completes and submits, an application for training, educational funding or other ISET supports:
↳ ↳ Application on website: www.nwac.ca
↳ ↳ Walk-in
↳ ↳ Job Fair
↳ ↳ Community Event
↳ ↳ Referral from Band or other organization
Tip: Capture the intake source in the client file (program system) (web, referral, event) so you can report outreach impact and follow up appropriately.
Client experience tip: Give applicants a simple checklist of required documents early to reduce back-and-forth.
Client Application
Reference: This slide reflects the client application form. Ensure applicants use the most current version approved by NWAC/PTMA.
Tip: If your tool supports it, link directly to the application and document checklist from this slide.
EI Consent Form
↳ Applicant MUST sign the 'Client Consent for EI Verification’ before the Request for EI Verification can be done.
↳ If an Applicant does not sign and submit the “Consent for EI Verification” their application CANNOT be processed.
EI Verification
↳ You must submit the 'EI Verification Request' to the Associate Director (or approved designate) to confirm the client’s eligibility for funding under EI or CRF.
↳ The signed 'Client Consent for EI Verification' MUST accompany the EI Request before any verification can be conducted in the LMDA system.
↳ NWAC will provide the Case Manager with the LMDA eligibility response within 2-3 business days of receipt of both the verification request and Client consent form.
Critical gate: EI verification requires signed consent first—do not attempt verification or submit a request without the consent on file.
Day-to-day: EI verification helps determine whether a client is eligible under the EI stream (often tied to EI Part II eligibility) or must be supported under CRF.
Timing tip: Tell clients this step usually takes a few business days once consent and request are submitted (per NWAC guidance).
Client Consent for EI Verification
EI Verification Request Form
Reference: These are the two key forms in the EI verification step (Client Consent + EI Verification Request).
Tip: Check forms for completeness (signature, date, client identifiers) before submitting to avoid delays.
Upon receipt of a new application you must immediately:
↳ Create a client file in the program system
↳ Add personal data from the application
↳ Create a new intake to mark the client as active (where your system uses activation)
↳ Assign the case manager
↳ Upload every document received from the applicant
↳ Record every interaction with the client in the client file
Recordkeeping habit: create the client file immediately on receipt—even before all documents arrive—so nothing is lost and follow-up is tracked.
Quality tip: use consistent file naming (e.g., “LOA_2025F”, “Fees_2025F”, “ID_StatusCard”, “Consent_EI_Verification”) to make reviews and audits easy.

You MUST contact applicant within five (5) business days to acknowledge receipt of their application and to request any missing information (this will be an automated process when the digital platform goes live).
You should advise clients their file will closed if documentation is not received by a ‘specified date’ in an email, or after 3 attempts made to request information.
Client will need to re-apply for funding if they do not respond and their file is closed. Client will go into the queue when their new application is received.
All requests and interactions need to be documented by emails and, also detailed in the ‘All requests and interactions must be recorded in the client file, with copies of key communications retained.
Client service tip: Acknowledge quickly and clearly—what you received, what’s missing, the deadline, and what happens if there’s no response.
Documentation tip: Store client communications (emails/letters) and summarize key points in case notes in the client file.
↳ Client Applications MUST be processed within three (3) weeks* of receipt of all the required documents from the applicant. (* dependent upon volume)
↳ Conduct thorough review of application, including (Employability Dimensions):
↳ ↳ Client training and employment goals;
↳ ↳ Review previous education and training;
↳ ↳ Current resume; and,
↳ ↳ Research Education, Training and Employment Pathways
Timeline clarity: The 3-week processing expectation starts after the file is complete (all required documents received).
Practical tip: Use a short processing checklist (eligibility, EI/CRF, documents, employability dimensions, research, recommendation) to stay consistent.
Your Client Files including the program system MUST be able to PASS AN AUDIT
Audit-ready means: the story of the file is obvious—eligibility decision, stream determination, approvals, payments, and case notes are all in the client file (program system) and consistent.
Tip: Before submitting to NWAC, do a ‘consistency scan’ (names, dates, amounts match across forms).
Ensure the secure handling of all confidential client information and adherence to privacy standards and protocols.
Maintain strict compliance with Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) standards as communicated by NWAC.

Ensure every client file is accurate, up-to-date, and uploaded into the program records database, including but not limited to, client application, supporting documentation, case notes, intervention financial details.
Privacy tip: Limit access to client information to those who need it, and avoid storing client data outside approved systems.
Data quality tip: If something changes (dates, costs, start date), update the program system and the funding documentation so records remain consistent.
Compliant File List

Suggested compliant file checklist (typical): application, eligibility/ID + self-declaration, EI verification consent + response, financial overview + verifications (if applicable), LOA + fees, case manager assessment + recommendation, NWAC approval, signed funding agreement, payment records/receipts, monthly attendance reports (if living allowance), case notes + outcomes.

chunks.title: Module 5 — Before approval: pending status, ID, consents, and tax reminders

items: Module 5 focuses on what must be in place before funding is considered approved: pending status, identity requirements, client consents, and tax reminders.
Case Manager MUST advise Clients that their application for funding is considered ‘pending’ until:
↳ The Client has provided all the requested documentation;
↳ The Case Manager has assessed the application and made their recommendation;
↳ The Case Manager has submitted entire client file and Assessment to NWAC (Associate Director/Senior Director) for review;
↳ NWAC approves and signs the Assessment; and,
↳ The ‘Client Funding Agreement’ has been signed by both the Client and the Case Manager.
Client messaging: ‘Pending’ means we are still collecting documents and completing review—funding is not approved until NWAC signs off and the funding agreement is signed.
Workflow tip: Use a consistent the program system status and note template so staff and clients get the same message every time.
Clients are to submit two (2) pieces of identification with their application and one MUST be Status/Treaty card along with the “Indigenous Self-Declaration form.
If a client does not have a Status/Treaty card then they MUST provide two (2) reference letters from Indigenous leadership from their registered Nation and/or community.
There are many reasons why an applicant may not have a Status/Treaty card.
We need to be diligent in our efforts to confirm access to ISET funding is legitimate. The self-declaration is not enough.
Identity verification tip: Store the two IDs and self-declaration together and record what was reviewed and when.
Client support tip: Be prepared to explain why self-declaration alone is not enough (program integrity and fairness).
Case Manager MUST review, “Client Acknowledgement of Funding Source” with client and obtain their signature.

Case Manager to advise client that any false or misleading statements and/or omission of information may be grounds for immediate suspension of any funding and may result in a repayment of funds to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), for monies received to which they were not entitled.
Practical risk reminder: Ensure clients understand that false statements or omissions can lead to suspension and repayment—communicate this respectfully and document that it was reviewed.
Tip: Encourage clients to disclose other funding sources early to avoid ‘double-dipping’ issues later.
Client Funding Agreement
Authorization for the Release of ISET Client Information
Client Acknowledgement of Funding Source
Consent for Use of Images Video and Audio
Client Conflict of Interest Declaration
Quick guide: Review what each form is for and when it’s required (some before verification, some after approval).
Tip: Missing signatures are a top cause of delays—use a sign-off checklist when meeting the client.
Case Manager MUST advise clients that they will be issued a T4A for ALL funding provided under the ISET program.
Clients MUST declare any amounts on their personal income tax return.
CRA is the entity responsible for determining tax exemption status, NOT Case Managers, PTMAs or NWAC.
Client support tip: Many clients are anxious about taxes—keep the message simple: they will receive a T4A and must report it; CRA decides exemption status.
Practice tip: Avoid offering tax advice; refer clients to CRA resources or a tax clinic if needed.
Module 6 covers financial disclosure and verification—this is where many files become delayed if documents are incomplete.
Applicant MUST complete the ‘Financial Overview’ document.
Documentation and proof of financial situation IS REQUIRED prior to any approval of funding.
To qualify for ISET funding, applicants must disclose ALL household income or funding received from all sources.
Verification of monthly expenses WILL be required for clients requesting a living allowance subsidy.
Case Manager to advise client their application WILL NOT be processed until the Overview document is completed and all verification documents requested, have been submitted.
Case Manager MUST verify income and expenses prior to recommending a living allowance.
Operational rule: Do not recommend living allowance until income and expenses are verified and documented (per NWAC guidance).
Client experience tip: Explain upfront that financial documents protect the client and the program by preventing overpayment/repayment situations.
Financial Overview
Reference: This is the Financial Overview form. Use it as the master summary of household income and essential expenses.
Tip: Keep the completed overview and all verification documents together in the client file (program system) so reviewers can validate quickly.
If Client is employed, they MUST provide:
↳ ↳ Copies of their last 3 paystubs
If Client is married, or equivalent, they MUST provide:
↳ ↳ Copies of partner’s last 3 paystubs
If Client has dependent children, they MUST provide:
↳ ↳ copy of their latest child tax benefit statement
↳ ↳ Verification of permanent disability and cost if child aged 12+
↳ If Client is in receipt of Alimony or Child Support, they MUST provide:
↳ ↳ ↳ Proof of payment for the previous four (4) months;
↳ ↳ ↳ Copy of the Maintenance Enforcement records showing the child support and/or alimony payments;
↳ ↳ ↳ If no legal documentation is available, the Client can provide proof of payment (bank statement) and a signed statement from both parties detailing child support and/or alimony arrangements.
Verification tip: Use the ‘last 3 paystubs’ rule consistently and document exceptions (e.g., new job, irregular income).
Practical tip: For child support/alimony, record whether the arrangement is formal (maintenance enforcement) or informal and what proof was provided.
A Client in receipt of social assistance MUST provide:
↳ a letter from their caseworker indicating how much they are receiving monthly and the amount of ‘top up’ they may be eligible to receive through the ISET program.
↳ Any regional/provincial requirements are the responsibility of the PTMA ISET Case Manager to fulfill prior to sending client file to NWAC.
If a Client is receiving funding from other sources, they MUST disclose the amounts, source(s), and provide documentation confirming amounts.
Other forms of income verification may be requested and can include but is not limited to:
↳ T4 or income tax assessments (3 years);
↳ Bank statements (3 months);
↳ Record of Employment (ROE);
↳ letter from current employer
Social assistance tip: The caseworker letter should confirm monthly amount and any rules about ‘top up’—ensure local requirements are met before submission to NWAC.
Completeness tip: Ask about *all* other funding sources early (Band funding, scholarships, other programs) to avoid later conflicts.
A Client requesting funding will be asked to provide proof of monthly expenses:
Childcare:
For children under the age of 12 – proof of the monthly childcare costs to the provider.
For children 12 years of age or older - childcare costs can be considered if the dependent child has a permanent disability.
↳ Documentation of care that is needed and amount required.
Childcare eligibility tip: For older children, disability-related care must be supported by documentation and tied to participation in the intervention.
Practical tip: Confirm the childcare provider cost and payment arrangement so the expense is verifiable.
Rent or Mortgage:
Client is to provide a copy of the rent/residence fees* or mortgage agreement *(client’s name MUST be on lease or other documentation).
Utilities:
Client is to submit copies of recent basic utility bills for the past three (3) months (power, natural gas, water, sewer, and garbage).
↳ Cable, satellite, and internet* are not considered basic utilities.
Housing cost tip: Ensure the client’s name appears on the lease/fees documentation; otherwise document the living arrangement and how costs are shared.
Utilities tip: Keep “basic utilities” separate from non-basic services like cable/internet, as per guidance.
Transportation:
Proof of the monthly expense for a public transit pass

If no access to public transportation, a client must submit proof of kilometres travelled per day and provide a copy of their Personal Liability/Property Damage vehicle insurance documents indicating they have coverage for use of personal vehicle.
Regional kilometer rates will apply (please speak with NWAC if unsure of regional rate).
Transportation tip: If using kilometres, document the calculation (km/day × days/month × regional rate) and store proof of insurance.
Escalation tip: If you’re unsure of the regional km rate, confirm with NWAC and note the confirmed rate in the file.

chunks.title: Module 7 — Living allowance (needs-based support during training)

items: Module 7 explains living allowance. The goal is fair, needs-based support during training while avoiding overpayments and repayment risk.
There is NO minimum (or flat rate) amount for a living allowance.
↳ Each client application MUST be assessed on its own merits. Providing ‘minimum’ amounts to clients who may not be eligible can put them at risk of having to repay those funds.
A living allowance MAY be provided on a ‘needs basis’ to a client participating in a training/educational intervention.
A living allowance is generally intended to help cover basic needs DURING (not before) the intervention starts and while the client is attending a training/educational institution.
A living allowance is a subsidy and is NOT intended to cover all a client’s monthly expenses or a deficit.
Back-dating a living allowance payment is NOT permissible under any circumstances.
Core concept: living allowance is discretionary and needs-based—there is no flat rate and it is not retroactive.
Practical approach: calculate the allowable basic-cost gap during the intervention period and document how you arrived at the recommended amount.
Client messaging tip: explain that living allowance is a subsidy for basic needs during training, not full income replacement.
Clients MUST disclose ALL household income/revenue from all sources.
The ‘Financial Overview’ MUST be completed and signed by the Client.
Income Verification IS REQUIRED prior to any approval of funding.
Coordinator MUST request documentation to verify monthly income and expenses prior to recommending a living allowance.
A Client on an active EI claim is NOT eligible for a living allowance until their claim is completed.
A living allowance will NOT be paid until the ‘Client Monthly Attendance Report’ has been completed and signed by the Client and verified by the Coordinator.
Gate: Active EI Part I claim = no living allowance until claim ends (per NWAC guidance). Plan supports accordingly.
Monthly control: attendance reports are required before payment—build this into your monthly routine and client expectations.
If eligible, a living allowance is intended to subsidize:
↳ Rent/mortgage payment;
↳ Monthly basic utilities (gas, water, hydro, sewer);
↳ Groceries;
↳ Transportation (bus/train pass)* - refer to previous slide
↳ Childcare**
*A Transportation subsidy is not intended to cover car payments, insurance or vehicle maintenance.

**Childcare is only eligible if their current monthly expense increases as a direct result of the client’s training or educational program. Eligibility will be determined on a case-by-case basis – refer to previous slide.
PLEASE NOTE:
A living allowance is not intended to cover a client’s previous debts (i.e., credit cards, student loans, bank loans, etc.).

Other expenses not eligible include such items as security systems, pet care, cellphones, entertainment, subscriptions, annual fees for certifications or licenses (outside of an active intervention), etc. (this is not a complete list of ineligible expenses).
Clarity tip: Separate ‘eligible basic needs’ from ‘not eligible’ costs when explaining to clients to reduce misunderstandings.
Documentation tip: For childcare, record the baseline cost and the incremental training-related increase to justify eligibility.
A living allowance is NOT to be processed for payment until the ‘Client Monthly Attendance Report’ has been completed and signed by the Client and verified by the Coordinator.

Coordinator MUST advise clients that any false or misleading statements on their Attendance Report will be grounds for immediate suspension of their living allowance and may result in a repayment of funds for monies received to which they were not entitled.
Clients MUST report all absences and, in some cases may be required to provide medical documentation to support absences from school, training or paid work placement.
Each month, the Coordinator MUST attach the client’s attendance report to the EFT form for which the monthly allowance is to be paid and submit for payment.
Operational routine: collect attendance report → verify → attach to EFT request → submit for payment. Do this consistently each month.
Absence handling tip: document absences and any required medical documentation, and record your follow-up actions.
Client Monthly Attendance Report
Reference: This is the Client Monthly Attendance Report. Store a signed copy each month in the client file (program system) alongside the EFT/payment record.

chunks.title: Module 8 — Eligible expenses and documentation standards

items: Module 8 covers what expenses are eligible and what documentation is required to support payments.
Tuition for an approved course or program at an accredited public or private training or educational institution or employment-related expenses are eligible for funding.
↳ Essential skills and upgrading programs as part of an intervention
↳ Eligible and recognized diploma/certificate programs;
↳ Four (4) year degree programs;
↳ Career counselling, job search activities, self-employment services; or,
↳ Master’s Programs may be considered on a case-by-case basis, and on funding availability.

Program-related expenses MAY also be eligible for funding such as, books, materials, clothing and supplies, exam fees, license or certificate fees, specialized equipment (computer*), criminal records checks, vulnerable-sector checks (this list is not complete).
Eligibility tip: Tie every funded expense to either (a) a direct training requirement or (b) an employment-related barrier addressed by the intervention.
Documentation tip: Keep proof for every expense (acceptance, fees, invoices, receipts, justification). If it isn’t documented, it will be treated as not eligible.
Clients MUST FIRST apply to their Band, Treaty Nation or Community before applying for ISET funding.
Band Denial Letter:
↳ Letter must be on official Band/Treaty Nation letterhead
↳ Letter must be current for the term/semester/year
↳ Program name in letter must match the request for funding
↳ It is not enough for client to say, “I missed the deadline”.
↳ Screenshots, written notes or the client’s word are not sufficient, nor compliant
Band Funding Letter:
↳ If the client receives funding for a ‘living allowance’ it makes them ineligible for a living allowance under ISET. ESDC considers this ‘double-dipping.
↳ Options if Band funding is insufficient
Band letter tip: Denial letters must be current, on letterhead, and match the program/term—screenshots and verbal statements are not sufficient.

Double-dipping risk: If Band funding includes a living allowance, the client is not eligible for ISET living allowance (per NWAC guidance). Document what Band funding covers and adjust your recommendation accordingly.
Clients MUST provide a Letter of Acceptance from an accredited educational or training institution with their application:
↳ Letter must be on official letterhead
↳ Letter must be current for the term/semester/year
↳ Program name in letter must match the request for funding
For multi-year programs, annual enrolment confirmation must be provided if funding is being requested through ISET.
Screen shots, written notes, and client’s word are not sufficient, nor compliant.
Acceptance letter tip: confirm term/year, program name match, and that the institution is accredited/recognized.
Multi-year programs: set a calendar reminder to request annual enrolment confirmation before continuing funding.
Clients MUST provide a Statement of Tuition and Fees from the accredited educational and training institution.
↳ Statement must be on official letterhead or a print-out from the student portal
↳ Statement must be current for the term/semester/year for which funding is being requested
Books – syllabus or a print-out from the student portal
Fees tip: ensure the statement shows tuition/fees for the specific term being funded and includes the student number if available.
Books/materials: retain syllabus/portal printout showing required materials to support eligibility.
Tuition and related course/program costs will be paid directly to the educational institution or training provider, where possible, upon approval of funding.

Statement of Tuition or invoice MUST be provided and include the student number, prior to any payment being made to the educational institution, and only for those approved amounts in the ‘Client Funding Agreement’.
The payee must be the same as the institution or person providing the training unless a letter is provided outlining different payment terms/payee.
Reimbursement directly to the Client will only be paid for approved and eligible costs as detailed in the ‘Client Funding Agreement’ and for which the Client can provide original ‘paid’ receipts.
Payment control: pay providers directly where possible; reimburse clients only for costs explicitly approved in the funding agreement with original paid receipts.
Payee tip: if payee differs from provider, store the letter explaining payment terms to prevent payment disputes.
Applicant MUST provide a letter from the training or educational institution stating that they require a specific piece of equipment or computer.
There is NO minimum (or flat rate) amount for specialized equipment or computers. Each request needs to be assessed on its own merits – Discretionary.
Client must submit a quote for the equipment/computer; however, any quote over $650 (Cdn.) must have the prior approval of NWAC.
The client MUST submit a receipt within 2 weeks of funding for the purchase if funding was advanced for the purchase.

↳ If no receipt is received, the client will be in a repayment situation. If applicable, any other funding provided to the client will be reduced accordingly until such time as the receipt is received.
Equipment tip: require the institution letter + quote; quotes over $650 require prior NWAC approval (per guidance).
Repayment risk: if funds are advanced, receipts must be returned within 2 weeks—set a reminder and follow up proactively.
There are supports available for Clients with disabilities which may be eligible for funding.
Funding will be determined on a case-by-case basis – there is no cap on the amount of funding – discretionary.

A Client MAY be eligible to receive funding support while participating in an intervention, for the provision of care for those solely dependent upon the Client. Eligibility will be determined on a case-by-case basis.
Disability supports: assess barriers and required supports case-by-case and document how each support enables participation in the intervention.
Dependent care: document dependency and why additional care is required for the client to participate in the intervention.
Your Client Files MUST be able to PASS AN AUDIT including the program system
Reminder: audit readiness is built through consistent documentation habits in the client file (program system)—do not leave uploads or notes until the end of the file.

chunks.title: Module 9 — Assessment, approval, and funding agreements

items: Module 9 covers how to write assessments and recommendations that are clear, consistent, and approvable.
The Case Manager Assessment needs to include an Overview of the Client's Application.

↳ Client Application Overview should include information about the client, their previous education, work experience, any specific information that will help in the review of their eligibility by NWAC.
↳ ↳ The Overview should not just state what supports the applicant is requesting.
↳ The Case Manager MUST ensure all the information, numbers and dates are consistent on all documentation. Any discrepancies will delay the review/approval process.
↳ Specifics of any previous ISET intervention MUST be included. It is not enough for a "yes" and/or a ‘year’. You will need to check the program’s records.
Assessment tip: write the ‘story of the file’—who the client is, what they are trying to achieve, what supports are requested, and why it makes sense.
Consistency rule: amounts, dates, and program details must match across all documents and the program system; check prior interventions in the client file (program system), not just client memory.
The Case Manager shall provide their recommendation for funding based on the application, documentation, research and conversations with the Client.
Recommendation must align with eligibility and funding criteria as established by ESDC and/or these guidance modules.

Recommendation must include 'justification' for the decision; not just, “I recommend we fund this client.” It should include such justification as, “I spoke with the Client and understand their goals, career path; I researched x, y, z; etc.”
The Case Manager does not have to recommend to fund every application or to provide a living allowance.
The Case Manager may recommend an alternate intervention:
↳ Alternate Funding Stream;
↳ Referral to another Agency;
↳ Employment Counselling / Job Search;
↳ Coaching / Mentoring;
↳ Different training/educational program that better aligns with client’s long-term career/employment goals.
Recommendation tip: include evidence (client goals + research + documentation) and be explicit about what you recommend and why.
Coordinator discretion: it’s okay to recommend alternate interventions or decline costs that don’t align with the pathway—document your rationale respectfully.
Case Manager Assessment
Reference: This is the Case Manager Assessment form/template. Use it to structure your overview and keep your recommendation defensible and easy to review.
ALL Case Manager recommendations MUST be submitted to NWAC for Approval.
NWAC will within 5 days respond to the Case Manager Recommendation to:
↳ Approve to fund Client as Recommended by Case Manager;
↳ Deny to fund Client with an explanation for decision;
↳ Meet with the Case Manager to review Recommendation, look at options, make amendments or request additional details; and request Case Manager to resubmit Recommendation, if appropriate; and,
↳ Case Manager will communicate decision to client.
Workflow: submit recommendations to NWAC; expect approve/deny/request-changes outcomes. Document the NWAC decision and your communication to the client.
Client messaging tip: communicate decisions clearly, including next steps or options if denied.
Upon NWAC Approval of the Recommendation to fund a client, the Case Manager shall complete the 'Client Funding Agreement'.
The Agreement MUST include the same amounts as detailed in the 'approved’ Case Manager Recommendation, without exception.
The Case Manager MUST meet with the Client to review the Funding Agreement and both the Case Manager and Client must sign the document.
Control point: the Funding Agreement must exactly match the NWAC-approved amounts—do not change amounts without re-approval.
Client meeting tip: review the agreement in plain language (what is covered, what isn’t, receipts/attendance expectations, repayment triggers).
Client Funding Agreement
Reference: This is the Client Funding Agreement. Store the fully signed version in the client file (program system) and ensure the client receives a copy.

chunks.title: Module 10 — Reporting, EI Section 25/ATQ, hardship, program records, contacts

items: Module 10 covers reporting, minimum service tracking, EI Section 25/ATQ concepts, hardship/repayment, and system compliance.

As the ISET Case Manager, you are responsible to provide NWAC with reports satisfactory to NWAC in scope and detail, concerning the progress of the ISET Program for your region(s), including information collected with respect to the applicants and clients.
Maintain the ‘ISET Advance and Active Client Spreadsheet’ and update the status of each client intervention as required, including:
↳ Client name; start and end date of intervention, intervention type, training institution; program name; related intervention costs; and, the date payment was made
↳ Submit Active Client List spreadsheet to NWAC at a minimum of every 90 days (10th day following the quarter) or more frequently if requested
↳ Track financial ISET advances from NWAC and report on eligible program expenses against advances received
↳ Submit narrative and statistical reports, including outcomes and program impacts at a minimum of every 90 days or more frequently as may be requested
↳ If applicable, work with your Finance staff to complete the Assessment and Claim Form.
Reporting routine: update the Active Client Spreadsheet continuously (not just quarterly) so reporting isn’t a scramble.

ILMP submissions: when action plans/interventions are activated and when they are closed, ensure the required ILMP information is captured and uploaded to the ESDC portal according to NWAC’s reporting schedule and guidance.
Financial oversight tip: track advances vs eligible expenditures and keep supporting documents organized for claims and audits.
ISET advance and active Client Spreadsheet
Reference: Active Client Spreadsheet. Recommended practice: one row per intervention, with clear start/end dates and cost totals that tie back to payments.

ALL ISET Program inquiries must be tracked on the Minimum Level Service Report Spreadsheet and submitted to the Senior Director, Economic Development. These inquiries are included in the ISET Annual Operating Plan submitted to ESDC.
Services are provided to clients that do not incur a cost to the ISET program:
↳ How to apply to the ISET program for funding;
↳ Requested an application or directed to website;
↳ Ask to use the computer/internet for job searches, resume writing, etc. ;
↳ Access to Labour Market Information;
↳ Referred to another agency.
Minimum service tracking: log all inquiries and no-cost supports (applications, job search help, LMI access, referrals). These counts feed annual planning/reporting.
Tip: Create a quick intake category list so staff categorize inquiries consistently.
Minimum Service Level Report
Reference: Minimum Service Level Report. Use it as a running log and submit on schedule per NWAC direction.
Section 25 Authority

While in receipt of EI Part I benefits, clients must be available, capable, and actively seeking employment. If a client is attending a training or employment activity which they have initiated on their own, they may be deemed “unavailable” and therefore would not receive EI Part I benefits.

Section 25 Authority (S25A) authorizes the ISPs to refer active EI Part I claimants to attend approved courses or programs of instruction. ISPs may also recommend that they participate in any other employment activity (interventions) designed to facilitate their re-entry into the labour force while maintaining entitlement to Part I benefits (staying on their active EI Part I benefit claim).
S25A also allows the ISP to counsel a client to leave their employment (Authorization to Quit) to take part in an approved employment or training intervention if:
a client has received a notice of imminent lay-off
a client must leave their current job for medical reasons, and they face an employment barrier to obtaining new employment

Typically, the Authorization to Quit (ATQ) or leave employment is only done while in an active Case Management situation, and typically within 2 weeks prior to the start date of the intervention. (The ATQ is not retroactive).
Take Note: The Authorization to Quit is used only in extenuating circumstances!

Plain-language: Section 25 referrals allow an authorized designated authority to refer EI claimants to training so they can remain eligible for EI Part I while attending approved training (where applicable).
ATQ caution: Authorization to Quit is exceptional and is typically used shortly before training starts; it is not retroactive.
Tip: Always follow your delegation list and NWAC direction—when uncertain, escalate before issuing an ATQ or referral.
Authorizing a Client to Quit and the Training Referral

An action plan is developed once a preliminary needs assessment is done with a client (based on information about the client’s work history and employment earnings), and the client signs the consent form and enters into case management. This action plan outlines the employment and training interventions that the client intends to participate in. Then the ISP can initiate the process to authorize the client to quit their employment to attend an ISET Program.

The ISP would complete and sign an Authorization to Quit (in writing, using the ATQ form and providing an explanation) to support that the individual has been approved (referred) to attend the ISET training or employment intervention. A copy of the ATQ form must be provided to the client and the EI processing centre (through their regional process).
The client will then apply for EI Part I and submit a copy of the ATQ along with their Records of Employment.
ESDC will review an application for EI Part I benefits and will approve if an individual meets all qualifying requirements and entitlement conditions.

The ATQ input cannot be done on the EIBIS system. However, by doing a query with the client’s SIN in EIBIS, the system will send a response to the ISP to advise if/when the client’s EI Part I Claim is finalized. The Training Referral can then be entered into the EIBIS, if the client’s application is finalized and deemed eligible.

ATQs involve a high level of responsibility. Ultimately, the authority or decision to allow an individual to quit their employment lies with the ISET ISP. EI does not make the determination whether the quit is “permitted”. However, it can refuse this authority if the requirements of S25 are not met (for example, the S25A isn’t identified on the ISPs delegation list, the ATQ was back-dated, etc.).
Process tip: ensure the client is in active case management with a documented action plan before initiating ATQ/referral steps.
System tip: document dates carefully (quit date, intervention start date, consent date) because retroactive ATQs are a common compliance failure point.
ESDC - Authorization to Quit
Reference: This slide points to ESDC Authorization to Quit guidance/material. Use the most current NWAC-approved process and documentation.
HARDSHIP POLICY
Repayment Agreement
Hardship/repayment: when overpayments or ineligible costs occur, address quickly with respectful communication, documented decisions, and a repayment agreement where required.
Tip: Escalate hardship and repayment situations early so the client receives consistent messaging and supports.
Program records and client files
↳ Case Managers must enter all client files received (funded or unfunded) into the program system.
↳ Case Managers must include required applicant data, case notes, and uploaded client documents per NWAC protocols.
↳ NWAC National Office will conduct file reviews to ensure new applications have been entered and meet ESDC program data requirements.
↳ Non-compliance issues will be addressed by the Senior Director.
↳ A monthly report may be provided to NWAC leadership/Board on compliance issues and overall program status.
Operational tip: run a monthly file completeness check—new intakes entered, missing documents flagged, notes up to date, and interventions/action plans correctly opened/closed for reporting.
Reporting tip: keep action plan and intervention status current so ILMP submissions and quarterly reports can be produced accurately.
Use these contacts for escalations, approvals, policy interpretation questions, and system/compliance issues that you cannot resolve regionally.
QUESTIONS?
End of module set. Use your tool’s search to find topics quickly (e.g., “living allowance”, “EI verification”, “Band letter”, “TWS”).
If you still have questions, escalate using the contacts provided and document the guidance you receive in the client file (program system) for future reference.
